label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
    Let $[\nabla]$ be a real oper. Then the intersection ${\bf Op}_n\cap {\bf M}_n^\mathbb R$ is transverse at $[\nabla]$.
head: environment

label: cor:main
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
The \emph{real locus} is defined by
$
    {\bf M}_n^{\mathbb R}=\left\{ [\nabla]\in {\bf M}_n \mid
    [\overline\nabla]=[\nabla]\right\}
$.
head: environment

label: prop:real
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:real}
    Let $
abla$ be irreducible and $\overline
abla=g(
abla)$.
    Then $g\overline g=\pm I$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
In the trivial frame (see \S \ref{sec:flat}), write $\nabla=d+B$. Then we have
    $$
    \overline B=g B g^{-1} - dg g^{-1} \ .
    $$
    Breaking into type, we have
$$
    \overline {B^{0,1}}=g B^{1,0}g^{-1}-\partial g g^{-1}\quad ,\quad
    \overline{B^{1,0}}=g B^{0,1}g^{-1}-\bar\partial g g^{-1} \ ,
$$
and hence,
    \begin{align*}
        B^{0,1}&=-\bar\partial {\bar g}{\bar g}^{-1}+\bar g\overline{B^{1,0}}{\bar
    g}^{-1} 
        =-\bar\partial {\bar g}{\bar g}^{-1}+\bar g
        \left(g B^{0,1}g^{-1}-\bar\partial g g^{-1}\right){\bar g}^{-1} \\
        &=-\bar\partial k k^{-1}+k B^{0,1}k^{-1}\ ,
    \end{align*}
    where $k=\bar g g$.
    A similiar calculation shows that $B^{1,0}=-\partial k k^{-1}+k
    B^{1,0}k^{-1}$. Hence, $d_\nabla(k)=0$. Since $\nabla$ is irreducible,
    $k$ must be constant and in the center of $\mathsf{SL}_n(\mathbb C)$. But then $k$ must
   also be real, and the conclusion follows.
head: environment

label: lem:real-holonomy
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:real-holonomy}
    Let $\nabla$ satisfy $\overline\nabla=g(\nabla)$, and let $\rho$ denote
    the holonomy of $\nabla$.
    Then there is $g_0\in \mathsf{SL}_n(\mathbb C)$ such that for all
    $\gamma\in\Gamma$,
    $\overline{\rho(\gamma)}=g_0\rho(\gamma)g_0^{-1}$.
head: environment

label: lem:form
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:form}
$H_
abla$  defines a hermitian form  on 
    $T_{[
abla]}{ f M}_n$ for any $[
abla]\in { f M}_n^\mathbb R$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first verify that $H_\nabla$ is hermitian. Indeed,
    using Proposition \ref{prop:real}, we have
    \begin{align*}
        \overline{H_\nabla(b_1,b_2)}&=-i\int_X \operatorname{tr}(\overline{b_1}\wedge
        \overline g^{-1}b_2\overline g) 
        =-i\int_X \operatorname{tr}(\overline{b_1}\wedge  gb_2 g^{-1}) 
        =-i\int_X \operatorname{tr}(g^{-1}\overline{b_1}g\wedge b_2 ) \\
        &=i\int_X \operatorname{tr}(b_2\wedge g^{-1}\overline{b_1}g) 
        =H_\nabla(b_2,b_1)\ .
\end{align*}
    Now suppose $b_1,b_2\in \ker d_\nabla$.
    Suppose that we change $b_2\to b_2+d_\nabla\eta$,
    for some endomorphism $\eta$.  Then 
    again using $\overline\nabla=g(\nabla)$, we have
    $\overline{b_2}\longrightarrow \overline{b_2}+d_{g(\nabla)}\overline\eta$.
    Now $d_{g(\nabla)}=\operatorname{Ad}_g\circ d_\nabla \circ \operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}$ and
    $d_\nabla b_1=0$,  and so the change in the integrand is
    $$
    \operatorname{tr}(b_1\wedge d_\nabla(\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}\overline\eta))
    =-d\operatorname{tr}(b_1 g^{-1}\overline\eta g) \ .
    $$
    A similar argument holds for a change $b_1\to b_1+d_\nabla\eta$.
    Hence, $H_{\nabla}$ is independent of the choice of representatives of
    $[b_1], [b_2]\in H^1_{d_\nabla}(X,\operatorname{ad}(E)))$.  
    Finally, if $\nabla_1=g_1(\nabla)$, then
    $\overline\nabla_1=(\overline{g_1}gg_1^{-1})(\nabla_1)$. 
    Under the isomorphism $H^1_{d_\nabla}(X,\operatorname{ad}(E))\xrightarrow{
   \,\smash{\raisebox{-0.5ex}{\ensuremath{\sim}}}\,}
    H^1_{d_{\nabla_1}}(X,\operatorname{ad}(E))$ given by $[b]\mapsto [\operatorname{Ad}_{g_1}b]$,
    we can compute that the hermitian form is invariant. This completes the proof.
head: environment

label: lem:real
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:real}
    Suppose $\nabla$ is an irreducible real connection.
    Let $[b]\in H^1_{d_\nabla}(X,\operatorname{ad}(E))$ be tangent to the real locus. Then
    $H_\nabla(b,b)=0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose we have a one parameter family $\nabla_t$ of connections satisfying 
    $\overline \nabla_t =g_t(\nabla_t)$, and set $b=\overset{\mathpalette\bigldot@{.5}}{\nabla}$, $h=\overset{\mathpalette\bigldot@{.5}}{g}
    g^{-1}$ at $t=0$.
    Then a calculation shows  that $\overline
    b=gbg^{-1}-d_{\overline\nabla}h$, or
    $$
    g^{-1}\overline b g=b-\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}d_{g(\nabla)}h=b-d_\nabla(g^{-1}hg) \
    .
    $$
Pairing this with $b$ in $H_\nabla$ gives zero, since 
$$
    \operatorname{tr}(b\wedge g^{-1}\overline b g)=\operatorname{tr}(b\wedge (b-d_\nabla(g^{-1}hg)))=
    d\operatorname{tr}(b\wedge g^{-1}hg) \ , 
$$
which then vanishes upon integration.
head: environment

label: prop:definite
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:definite}
    Suppose $\nabla$ is a real oper. Then $H_\nabla$ is definite on
    $T_{[\nabla]}{\bf Op}_n$ (with the sign depending on the sign of $g\overline
    g$ in Proposition  \ref{prop:real}.
head: environment

label: eqn:square
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $[b]\in T_{[\nabla]}{\bf Op}_n$. We choose a particular representative.
    In the frame ${\bf e}$, a variation of opers $\nabla=d+A$ is given by a family
    $Q_i+tq_i$, where $q_i$ are holomorphic $i$-differentials (locally). 
    Let $a=\overset{\mathpalette\bigldot@{.5}}{A}$. We may write this as: $a={\bf e}_n\otimes q^t$, where 
$$
    q^t=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1} q_{n-j+1}{\bf e}_j^\ast
$$
in the dual frame ${\bf e}^\ast$ to ${\bf e}$.
    In the frame ${\bf v}$, 
    $b=W^{-1} a W= (W^{-1}{\bf e}_n)\otimes q^t W $,
    where $W$ is as in \eqref{eqn:wronskian}.
    By Proposition \ref{prop:real}, $g\overline g=\epsilon I$, where
    $\epsilon^2=1$. Then:
    \begin{align*}
        i\operatorname{tr}(b\wedge g^{-1}\overline b g) &=
        i\operatorname{tr}\left((W^{-1}{\bf e}_n)\otimes q^t W \wedge
        g^{-1}(\overline{W^{-1}{\bf e}_n})\otimes \overline{q^t W} g
        \right) \\
        &=
        i\epsilon\operatorname{tr}\left((gW^{-1}{\bf e}_n)\otimes q^t W \wedge
        (\overline{gW^{-1}{\bf e}_n})\otimes \overline{q^t W} 
        \right)  \ .
    \end{align*}
    But in local coordinates, this last line may be written
    \begin{equation} \label{eqn:square} 
    =\epsilon \left| q^t W(\overline{gW^{-1}{\bf e}_n})\right|^2\, idz\wedge
    d\bar z \ .
    \end{equation} 
    This proves the semidefiniteness.  Assume now that
    $H_{\nabla}(b,b)=0$.  From \eqref{eqn:square}, 
$$q^t W(\overline{gW^{-1}{\bf e}_n})=0\ .$$
We wish to show that this implies $q=0$.
Using the induced connection on the dual bundle, along with
    $\overline\nabla=g(\nabla)$, we have
    \begin{align}
        0=d\left(q^t W(\overline{gW^{-1}{\bf e}_n})\right)
        &=d_\nabla(q^t W)(\overline{gW^{-1}{\bf e}_n})
        + (q^t W)(\overline{d_{\overline\nabla}(gW^{-1}{\bf e}_n}))\notag \\
        0&=d_\nabla(q^t W)(\overline{gW^{-1}{\bf e}_n})
        + (q^t W)(\overline{gd_{\nabla}(W^{-1}{\bf e}_n})) \label{eqn:key}
    \end{align}
    Taking the $(0,1)$ part in \eqref{eqn:key}, the first term vanishes
    because $q$ and $W$ are holomorphic. Since in the frame ${\bf v}$ the
    connection is trivial, we find that 
    $ (q^t W)(\overline{g{U'}})=0$,
    where $U=W^{-1}{\bf e}_n$.  Repeating this for the $k$-th derivatives
    $U^{(k)}$, we have 
    $q^tW(\overline{gU^{(k)}})=0$, $k=0,\ldots, n-1$.
    Now the result follows from Lemma \ref{lem:independent} below.
head: environment

label: lem:independent
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eqn:matrix
title: Proof
body_md:
By the discussion in \S \ref{sec:opers}, 
    we have $dW W^{-1}=-A$, or $d(W^{-1})=W^{-1}A$, where $A$ is given by
    \eqref{eqn:A}. For $j=1,\ldots, n$, set $U_j=W^{-1}{\bf e}_j$, so that $U=U_n$.  
    Then a computation shows that for all $j$,
    $$
     U_j^\prime=-U_{j-1}+Q_{n-j+1}U_n\ .
    $$
    where for convenience we set $Q_1=0$, $U_0=0$.
    It follows inductively that 
$$
    U_j^{(k)}=(-1)^kU_{j-k}+\sum_{i\geq n-i+1}f_i U_i \ .
    $$
    for functions $f_i$ involving $Q_j$'s and derivatives.
Hence, in particular, 
    \begin{equation} \label{eqn:matrix} 
    \left(\begin{matrix} U \\  U' \\ \vdots \\
    U^{(n-1)}\end{matrix}\right)=
    \left(\begin{matrix} 1 & 0 & \ldots & 0 \\
        0 & -1 & \ldots & 0 \\
        \ast &\ast & \ddots & \vdots \\
    \ast & \ast & \ast & (-1)^{n-1} \end{matrix}
    \right)
    \left(\begin{matrix} U_n \\  U_{n-1} \\ \vdots \\
    U_1\end{matrix}\right)
    \end{equation} 
Since $W$ is invertible, the vectors $U_1,\ldots, U_n$ are pointwise
    independent. Since the matrix in \eqref{eqn:matrix} is also invertible, 
    the result follows.
head: environment
